title_en: Chen Chengyu v. Inner Mongolia Changyu Stone Industry Co., Ltd. — contract dispute
ruling_gist_en: 1. Authenticity of seal does not equal authenticity of agreement. The act of forming an agreement and the act of affixing a seal are relatively independent in nature. The content of an agreement is a manifestation of the mutual consensus between parties, while the act of affixing a seal is the method by which each party confirms the content of such mutual consensus. The two are interrelated yet relatively independent. In terms of evidence, authenticity of a seal generally allows for a presumption of authenticity of the agreement. However, where there is evidence that negates or casts doubt on the authenticity of the act of forming mutual consensus, the authenticity of the agreement cannot be directly presumed based solely on the authenticity of the seal. In other words, the seal is merely prima facie evidence for proving the authenticity of an agreement, and the people's court must consider other evidence and facts comprehensively when determining the authenticity of the agreement.

full_text_en:
Chen Chengyu v. Inner Mongolia Changyu Stone Industry Co., Ltd. — Contract Dispute

Ruling Summary

I. The authenticity of a seal does not necessarily mean the authenticity of an agreement. The act of forming an agreement and the act of affixing a seal are relatively independent in nature. The content of an agreement is a manifestation of the mutual intent of the parties, while the act of affixing a seal is the method by which the parties confirm the content of their mutual agreement. The two are interrelated yet relatively independent. In evidentiary terms, the authenticity of a seal generally allows for the presumption of the agreement's authenticity. However, if there is evidence that denies or casts doubt on the authenticity of the act of forming the mutual intent, the authenticity of the agreement cannot be directly presumed based solely on the authenticity of the seal. In other words, a seal constitutes only prima facie evidence of the authenticity of an agreement. A people's court must comprehensively consider other evidence and facts in determining the authenticity of the agreement.

II. An expert opinion issued in another case tried by a people's court and raised by a party during the trial of the instant case may only be treated as ordinary documentary evidence. Pursuant to Articles 76 and 78 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, an expert opinion may only be applied for, formed, and used in accordance with the law within the trial of the instant case.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2014) Min Ti Zi No. 178

Re-Applicant (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Inner Mongolia Changyu Stone Industry Co., Ltd. Domicile: East side of National Highway 209, Chengguan Town, Helingeer County, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.

Legal Representative: Li Quansuo, General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Wang Zhihua, lawyer at Beijing Yuren Law Firm.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Chen Chengyu, male, Han ethnicity, born on January 9, 1964, domiciled in Fuding City, Fujian Province.

Agent ad litem: Shang Yonggui, lawyer at Inner Mongolia Hede Law Firm.

The re-applicant, Inner Mongolia Changyu Stone Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Changyu Company), dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2013) Min Min Zhong Zi No. 1266 rendered by the Fujian High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Fujian High Court) on December 9, 2013, in a contract dispute with the respondent, Chen Chengyu, applied to this Court for retrial. This Court rendered the civil ruling (2014) Min Shen Zi No. 168 on June 19, 2014, ordering the retrial of this case. After forming a collegial panel in accordance with the law, this Court held a hearing on September 2, 2014. Wang Zhihua, agent ad litem for Changyu Company, and Shang Yonggui, agent ad litem for Chen Chengyu, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The trial of this case is now concluded.

The Ningde Intermediate People's Court of Fujian Province (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance) found the following facts through trial: On May 1, 2005, Chen Chengyu and Changyu Company entered into an "Agreement" (hereinafter referred to as the May 1 Agreement), which clearly stipulated matters concerning the cooperative exploitation of porphyritic garnet-bearing black granite stone mines (hereinafter referred to as "granite mines") at Yushugou, Helingeer County, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. In November 2007, due to Chen Chengyu's breach of contract, Changyu Company filed a lawsuit with the Helingeer County People's Court of Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region (hereinafter referred to as Helingeer County Court), seeking dissolution of the May 1 Agreement. After trial, the Helingeer County Court rendered the civil judgment (2007) He Min Chu Zi No. 428-2, dissolving the May 1 Agreement. Chen Chengyu appealed, and the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court of Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region (hereinafter referred to as Hohhot Intermediate Court) rendered the civil judgment (2008) Hu Fa Min Er Zhong Zi No. 957, affirming the first-instance judgment, which has now become effective. On September 22, 2008, Chen Chengyu filed a lawsuit with the Hohhot Intermediate Court, seeking compensation from Changyu Company of RMB 9,000,000 for his investment in the mines. During the litigation of that case, the Hohhot Intermediate Court commissioned Inner Mongolia Xingyi United Accounting Firm (hereinafter referred to as Xingyi Accounting Firm) to authenticate the earth stripping and granite mining costs incurred by Chen Chengyu during his contract operation of the granite mines, and commissioned the Survey Team of Inner Mongolia Coal Mine Design Institute (hereinafter referred to as the Coal Mine Survey Team) to measure the earth and rock volumes excavated at each mine opening. Subsequently, Xingyi Accounting Firm issued the No. (2009) 002 "Authentication Report on Earth Stripping and Granite Mining Costs at Helingeer County Yushugou Granite Mine" (hereinafter referred to as the "Authentication Report"), determining that the earth stripping and granite mining costs incurred by Chen Chengyu during his contract operation of the granite mines amounted to RMB 7,112,080. Thereafter, because Chen Chengyu failed to pay the litigation fee on time, the Hohhot Intermediate Court rendered the civil ruling (2008) Hu Min Er Chu Zi No. 88 on February 28, 2011, ordering that the case be treated as withdrawn by Chen Chengyu. On November 1, 2011, Chen Chengyu filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance in this case, requesting that Changyu Company compensate him for his investment in the mines in the amount of RMB 7,112,080 based on the above Authentication Report. During the hearing on the jurisdictional objection in this case, the Fujian High Court commissioned a forensic examination of the authenticity of the official seal affixed to the "Supplementary Agreement" dated May 3, 2005 (hereinafter referred to as the May 3 Supplementary Agreement) provided by Chen Chengyu. Fujian Dingli Forensic Examination Center concluded upon examination that the impression of "Inner Mongolia Changyu Stone Industry Co., Ltd." on the examined document and the impression of "Inner Mongolia Changyu Stone Industry Co., Ltd." on the sample were made by the same seal. The Fujian High Court rendered the civil ruling (2012) Min Min Zhong Zi No. 368 on May 21, 2012, dismissing Changyu Company's appeal against the jurisdictional objection and affirming the original ruling.

The court of first instance held that, with respect to the issue of whether the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was ever signed by the parties, Changyu Company did not dispute the authenticity of the civil ruling (2012) Min Min Zhong Zi No. 368 and the "Forensic Examination Opinion." The court of first instance admitted these pieces of evidence and accordingly could determine the authenticity of Changyu Company's seal on the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. Changyu Company, claiming objections to the examination conclusion, applied for re-examination of the authenticity of the company seal on the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. However, it failed to provide evidence to prove that the examination opinion suffered from procedural violations or insufficient grounds for its conclusions. The court of first instance did not permit Changyu Company's application for re-examination. As for Changyu Company's application to examine the printing and sealing times of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement, the court of first instance held that since the authenticity of Changyu Company's seal on the agreement had been confirmed, even if the printing time of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was after the sealing, Changyu Company should still bear the legal consequences of its expression of intent. Changyu Company claimed that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was fabricated by Chen Chengyu using blank paper with the company seal affixed that he held, printed and used for litigation. However, Changyu Company failed to provide evidence to support its claim. Based on the existing evidence, the court of first instance determined that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was genuine and should represent the true expression of intent of Changyu Company. Regarding the issue of whether Changyu Company should compensate Chen Chengyu for his investment losses incurred during the performance of the May 1 Agreement, with respect to the Authentication Report, the letter of commission for forensic examination from the Hohhot Intermediate Court, and the "Explanation" issued by Xingyi Accounting Firm, Changyu Company did not dispute their authenticity upon cross-examination. The court of first instance admitted them and could use them as the basis for deciding the case. The contents of the "Receipts" and "Invoices" submitted by Chen Chengyu pertained to mining operation fees paid by Chen Chengyu to Changyu Company and were not relevant to this case. The court of first instance did not admit them. As for the nature of the Authentication Report, although the commission letter from the Hohhot Intermediate Court was expressed as a "letter of commission for forensic examination," the actual content commissioned by the court was a cost authentication. The Authentication Report was an authentication of Chen Chengyu's investment costs and was, in nature, a type of accounting authentication. Upon examination, Xingyi Accounting Firm, which performed the authentication, possessed the necessary auditing and authentication qualifications, and the authenticating personnel also had accounting qualifications. Although the authentication process used the "Survey Explanation for Yushugou Marble Mine" prepared by the Coal Mine Survey Team of the Inner Mongolia Coal Mine Design Institute and engaged engineering cost professional technicians to perform the authentication calculation, this constituted the accountant using expert assistance to perform the authentication service, which was consistent with the basic standards for certified public accountant authentication services and did not affect the legality of the authentication report. Moreover, the Coal Mine Survey Team was commissioned by the people's court to calculate the earth and rock volumes, and the personnel who performed the measurement and calculation also had the corresponding engineer qualifications. Changyu Company raised objections to the content of the Authentication Report but did not apply for re-authentication. Therefore, the court of first instance did not accept Changyu Company's arguments and confirmed the probative value of the Authentication Report. Consequently, the court of first instance found that the earth stripping and granite mining costs incurred by Chen Chengyu during his contract operation of the granite mines amounted to RMB 7,112,080. Changyu Company claimed that after signing the May 1 Agreement, Chen Chengyu subcontracted the mines to others and made no actual investment. However, the evidence submitted by Changyu Company did not meet the formal requirements for evidence, and Chen Chengyu denied this claim. Therefore, Changyu Company's claim lacked sufficient basis, and the court of first instance did not support it. In summary, the court of first instance held that the parties to a contract should perform their obligations in accordance with the contract. In this case, Chen Chengyu and Changyu Company signed the May 3 Supplementary Agreement on May 3, 2005, stipulating that upon dissolution of the May 1 Agreement, Changyu Company should settle and refund Chen Chengyu's investment costs. As authenticated by the accounting firm, the earth stripping and granite mining costs incurred by Chen Chengyu during his contract operation of the granite mines were determined to be RMB 7,112,080. Therefore, Chen Chengyu's claim for Changyu Company to refund the above investment costs in accordance with the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was legally grounded, and the court of first instance supported it. Changyu Company argued that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was not genuine and that Chen Chengyu had made no capital investment, but failed to provide effective evidence to substantiate its claims. The court of first instance did not accept this argument based on lack of factual basis. Accordingly, pursuant to Articles 8 and 97 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 64, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of first instance rendered judgment: Changyu Company shall pay Chen Chengyu RMB 7,112,080 within ten days from the effective date of this judgment. If the monetary payment obligation is not performed within the period specified in the judgment, interest on the debt for delayed performance shall be doubled in accordance with Article 253 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The court acceptance fee for the first instance was RMB 61,585, to be borne by Changyu Company.

After the first-instance judgment was rendered, Changyu Company, dissatisfied, appealed to the Fujian High Court, requesting that the original judgment be set aside, a new judgment be entered, and Chen Chengyu's claims be dismissed. The main grounds of appeal were: (1) The fact that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was signed by the parties does not exist. During the jurisdictional objection proceedings in this case, Changyu Company had applied to the court of second instance for a forensic examination of whether the official seal affixed to the May 3 Supplementary Agreement submitted by Chen Chengyu was consistent with the seal used by Changyu Company at the time and of its authenticity. The forensic examination document did not inform Changyu Company of its right to apply for reconsideration. The court of first instance also did not inform Changyu Company of its right to apply for re-examination, depriving it of its right to judicial remedy. Chen Chengyu stole blank paper with the company seal affixed and added the printed text later. Therefore, Changyu Company argued that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was fabricated after the Hohhot Intermediate Court lawsuit and was false. (2) From August 15, 2005 to September 26, 2006, Chen Chengyu had subcontracted the mine to others for exploitation. However, the Authentication Report found the actual construction period to be from 2005 to 2007. Therefore, the earth and rock volumes calculated based on the 2007 Metallurgical Mine Estimated Budget Quota in the report were not genuine, and the resulting mining costs were also inaccurate. The authentication institution for the No. (2009) 002 Authentication Report did not have engineering cost assessment qualifications. The Coal Mine Survey Team commissioned by the Hohhot Intermediate Court did not have the qualifications within its business scope to measure earth and rock volumes, and the engineering cost engineer in this authentication report was not an authenticating personnel of that institution. The court of first instance's classification of the Authentication Report as an accounting authentication was not in accordance with legal provisions. Accounting authentication is where certified public accountants issue conclusions that provide a certain level of assurance in written report form as to whether the information of the authenticated object conforms to appropriate standards in all material respects. Engineering cost refers to the total expenditure for carrying out a certain construction project, the core of which includes investment estimation, design budget estimate, revised budget estimate, construction drawing budget, project settlement, and final completion accounts. The Authentication Report provided by Chen Chengyu in the first instance clearly belonged to the latter.

Chen Chengyu argued in defense: (1) The May 3 Supplementary Agreement signed between Chen Chengyu and Changyu Company on May 3, 2005 objectively existed. During the appeal of the jurisdictional objection, Changyu Company applied to the Fujian High Court for a forensic examination, and the item to be examined was the seal impression on the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. The Fujian High Court commissioned Fujian Dingli Forensic Examination Center to conduct the examination, which issued a forensic examination opinion: "The impression of Inner Mongolia Changyu Stone Industry Co., Ltd. on the examined document and the impression of Inner Mongolia Changyu Stone Industry Co., Ltd. on the sample were made by the same seal." This examination opinion had already confirmed that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement signed by the parties on May 3, 2005 was objective and genuine. There was no legal basis for Changyu Company's demand that the forensic examination document inform it of its right to apply for reconsideration. Chen Chengyu argued that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was fabricated after the Hohhot Intermediate Court lawsuit and was false, but there was no evidence to support this. (2) The Authentication Report produced by Chen Chengyu in the first instance was lawfully prepared by a qualified accounting firm commissioned by the Hohhot Intermediate Court based on a large amount of original documents provided by Chen Chengyu. From May 1, 2005, until 2007, the parties signed a new agreement. The Authentication Report was precisely an authentication of the exploitation during the performance period of the parties' agreement. The Certified Public Accountants Law of China and the Basic Standards for Assurance Engagements of Certified Public Accountants of China clearly stipulate that assurance engagements are within the scope of business of certified public accountants; accounting firms may issue assurance reports; when performing assurance engagements on assurance objects, certified public accountants and accounting firms may use valuation and measurement methods; if an assurance engagement involves specialized knowledge and skills beyond the competence of certified public accountants, they may engage persons with specialized knowledge to assist them in performing the assurance engagement. From the content of the Authentication Report, it was precisely prepared by the accounting firm using valuation and measurement methods and engaging specialized personnel.

The court of second instance held that the issues in dispute in this appeal were: (1) Whether the first-instance trial procedure was lawful; (2) Whether the Authentication Report could be used as the basis for finding facts in this case.

(1) Regarding the issue of whether the first-instance trial procedure was lawful.

The court of second instance held that during the appeal of the jurisdictional objection in this case, Changyu Company applied to the Fujian High Court for a forensic examination, and the item to be examined was the seal impression on the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. The court of second instance commissioned Fujian Dingli Forensic Examination Center to conduct the examination, and the center had already issued a forensic examination opinion. Changyu Company's claim that the above forensic examination opinion required it to be informed of its right to apply for reconsideration had no legal basis. During the substantive trial of this case by the court of first instance, Changyu Company again applied for re-examination of the authenticity of the company seal on the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. Because it failed to provide evidence to prove that the forensic examination opinion of Fujian Dingli Forensic Examination Center suffered from procedural violations or insufficient grounds for its conclusions, the court of first instance's refusal to permit Changyu Company's application for re-examination was not improper. Changyu Company's claim that the court of first instance did not inform it of its right to apply for re-examination, thereby depriving it of its right to judicial remedy, had no legal basis. Additionally, during the first instance, Changyu Company applied to examine the printing and sealing times of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. Changyu Company claimed that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was fabricated by Chen Chengyu using blank paper with the company seal affixed that he held, printed and used for litigation. However, Changyu Company failed to provide evidence to support its claim. The court of first instance held that since the authenticity of Changyu Company's seal had been confirmed, further examination of the printing and sealing times of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement was meaningless, and thus it refused to permit Changyu Company's application for examination. The procedure was lawful.

(2) Regarding the issue of whether the Authentication Report could be used as the basis for finding facts in this case.

The court of second instance held that on May 1, 2005, Chen Chengyu and Changyu Company signed the May 1 Agreement, which stipulated matters concerning the cooperative exploitation of porphyritic garnet-bearing black granite stone mines at Yushugou, Helingeer County, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Chen Chengyu and Changyu Company also signed the May 3 Supplementary Agreement on May 3, 2005, stipulating that upon dissolution of the May 1 Agreement, Changyu Company should settle and refund Chen Chengyu's investment costs. After the dispute arose, the May 1 Agreement signed by the parties was dissolved by a court judgment in accordance with the law. On September 22, 2008, Chen Chengyu filed a lawsuit with the Hohhot Intermediate Court, claiming that Changyu Company should compensate him for his investment in the mines. During the litigation of that case, the Hohhot Intermediate Court commissioned Xingyi Accounting Firm to authenticate the earth stripping and granite mining costs incurred by Chen Chengyu during his contract operation of the granite mines. Xingyi Accounting Firm issued the No. (2009) 002 Authentication Report, determining that the earth stripping and granite mining costs incurred by Chen Chengyu during his contract operation of the Helingeer County Yushugou granite mine amounted to RMB 7,112,080. The Authentication Report was commissioned by the court in the exercise of its authority; the authenticating entity was an accounting firm as prescribed by relevant laws and regulations, and Xingyi Accounting Firm possessed the necessary auditing and authentication qualifications, and the authenticating personnel also had accounting qualifications; the content of the authentication was the costs incurred for earth stripping and granite mining during Chen Chengyu's contract operation of the Helingeer County Yushugou granite mine; the basis for the authentication was the "Metallurgical Mine Estimated Budget Quota 2007", the "Metallurgical Mine Construction and Installation Engineering Cost Quota 2007", and the "Survey Explanation for Yushugou Marble Mine" compiled by the Coal Mine Survey Team on May 19, 2009. Although the authentication process used the "Survey Explanation for Yushugou Marble Mine" and engaged engineering cost professional technicians to perform the authentication calculation, this constituted the accountant using expert assistance to perform the authentication service, which was consistent with the standards for certified public accountant authentication services. Furthermore, Changyu Company did not apply for re-authentication during the first instance trial of this case. Therefore, the above Authentication Report could be used as the basis for deciding the case in finding that Chen Chengyu had made investments in the disputed mine and the specific amount of costs incurred.

In summary, the court of second instance held that the facts found by the first-instance judgment were clear, the law was correctly applied, and the procedure was lawful, and should be affirmed. Changyu Company's grounds of appeal could not be established. Pursuant to Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court rendered judgment: Appeal dismissed, original judgment affirmed. The court acceptance fee for the second instance was RMB 61,585, to be borne by Changyu Company.

Changyu Company, dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2013) Min Min Zhong Zi No. 1266 of the Fujian High Court, applied to this Court for retrial. This Court rendered the civil ruling (2014) Min Shen Zi No. 168 on June 19, 2014, ordering the retrial of this case, formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law, and conducted a public hearing of this case on September 2, 2014.

Changyu Company stated in its retrial application: (1) The 5.3 Supplementary Agreement, which was the main evidence for the facts found in the original judgment, was forged by Chen Chengyu. (a) Changyu Company and Chen Chengyu never signed the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement. The two parties signed the 5.1 Agreement on May 1, 2005, regarding the cooperative mining contracting matters. During the execution of the agreement, due to Chen Chengyu's breach of contract, Changyu Company filed a lawsuit in 2007 with the Horinger County People's Court to rescind the 5.1 Agreement. In that case, Chen Chengyu, during his appeal and in the separate lawsuit for damages, never mentioned the existence of the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement until September 26, 2011, when Chen Chengyu filed the lawsuit with the court of first instance. Chen Chengyu's explanation that he had previously been unable to find the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement is unreasonable. Even if the document could not be found during the original litigation, it should have been mentioned. (b) Chen Chengyu had the possibility to forge the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement. During the second instance proceedings, although the seal on the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement was consistent with Changyu Company's seal, during the contracting process, Chen Chengyu had the opportunity and convenience to access and use the company seal. In the cooperation, Chen Chengyu also frequently used the company seal (for example, when handling civil explosive materials at the public security department, he used blank paper bearing the company seal or held the company seal). Therefore, Chen Chengyu had the possibility to forge the Supplementary Agreement by affixing the company seal to blank paper. (c) The 5.3 Supplementary Agreement has serious formal defects. First, the reversed positions of Party A and Party B violate customary rules. In contracts and similar instruments, it is a general civil customary rule that the corporate legal person or the employer is Party A, and the individual or contractor is Party B. In the 5.1 Agreement signed by the two parties and several previous agreements, Changyu Company was Party A and Chen Chengyu was Party B. However, in the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement, signed only two days later, Changyu Company's position was reversed to Party B and Chen Chengyu became Party A. This does not conform to general civil customary rules. The only explanation for this reversal is that the blank paper bearing Changyu Company's seal had the seal affixed in the lower right corner. Due to the limitation of the seal's position on this paper, Changyu Company could only be placed in the position of Party B. Second, there is no signature of Wang Maotang, the legal representative of Changyu Company. According to the 5.1 Agreement signed by the parties, that agreement not only bore Changyu Company's seal but also the signature of company head Wang Maotang, which satisfies the requirements for the agreement's validity and is consistent with common practice. The 5.3 Supplementary Agreement provided by Chen Chengyu does not have Wang Maotang's signature for confirmation. Third, the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement does not contain a clause regarding the number of copies of the agreement. The final clause of the 5.1 Agreement signed by the parties states, "This agreement is made in duplicate, with equal legal effect," which is a general clause that an agreement should contain. The 5.3 Supplementary Agreement provided by Chen Chengyu does not have this clause, nor does it stipulate that the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement has the same legal effect as the 5.1 Agreement. Currently, Chen Chengyu has provided only one copy of the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement. Changyu Company does not have such an agreement at all. Chen Chengyu also failed to adduce evidence that Changyu Company holds the same 5.3 Supplementary Agreement, making it difficult to corroborate the objective authenticity of the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement. (d) The content of the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement is contrary to common sense, and the rights and obligations are manifestly unfair. It does not represent the true intention of Changyu Company. First, according to the content and principles of the 5.1 Agreement signed by the parties on May 1, 2005, regarding the mining cooperation, the two parties were engaged in cooperative mining. Changyu Company held the Mining License and was the mining right holder. Chen Chengyu was the user, with a contracting operation nature. According to the contract, Chen Chengyu was to independently mine and sell products and independently obtain operating profits, bearing his own risks. The compensation for the use of the mine that Changyu Company was to receive under the agreement was essentially the contract fee collected by the employer, with a fixed amount (RMB 300,000 per year for the first three years and RMB 500,000 per year starting from the fourth year). The rights and obligations in this agreement were basically fair. However, the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement stipulated that regardless of whether Changyu Company had the right to terminate, Changyu Company was liable to compensate Chen Chengyu for his investment. Such a stipulation clearly violates the principle of equality and consistency of rights and obligations between the two parties. Second, after the termination of the mining contracting agreement, according to the allocation of rights and obligations in contracting operations, the general practice is that no further mine usage fees are collected. It is not possible to compensate Chen Chengyu for his investment losses when Chen Chengyu had already mined and sold products. Third, the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement interprets that "losses upon termination" under the 5.1 Agreement refers only to Chen Chengyu's operating losses, excluding his investment. This is self-contradictory. So-called operating losses encompass the issues of input (or investment) and output. The phrase "operating losses shall be borne by oneself" inherently includes the implication that investment after termination is borne by oneself. This contradicts the stipulation that investment must be borne by Changyu Company. The content itself is inconsistent and further indicates that the agreement was forged. Fourth, in contracting operations, where Chen Chengyu breached the contract and Changyu Company lawfully rescinded it, requiring Changyu Company to compensate Chen Chengyu for his investment, with the investment being uncertain, such a mode of rights and obligations violates fairness. According to the 5.1 Agreement, Changyu Company was to collect compensation of RMB 300,000 per year from Chen Chengyu for the first three years of the contract period and RMB 500,000 per year starting from the fourth year. However, the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement imposes on Changyu Company the burden of compensating Chen Chengyu for investments of several million or even tens of millions. When the investment does not materialize into equipment or buildings but is directly converted into products that are sold, requiring Changyu Company to bear such investment losses is contrary to common sense. In summary, the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement has obvious formal defects, its content is contrary to common sense, the rights and obligations are manifestly unfair, and it was forged by Chen Chengyu using blank paper bearing the company seal. It does not represent the true intention of Changyu Company. (e) The jurisdiction of the case does not comply with legal provisions. At the time indicated in the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement for its signing and during the 2007 litigation between the parties in the Horinger County People's Court, Chen Chengyu's domicile was at Xinhua Street North Community, Taiyuan City, Shanxi Province, not Fuding City, Fujian Province. According to the law, the place of household registration is not the chosen jurisdiction under the contract. Moreover, the jurisdiction clause in the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement, which places the jurisdiction for a possible compensation dispute in Chen Chengyu's own place of household registration, thousands of miles away, not only is inconvenient for handling the dispute between the parties but is also unreasonable given that Chen Chengyu was not in a dominant contractual position at the time of signing. The only reasonable explanation for placing the litigation jurisdiction in the contractor Chen Chengyu's place of household registration in the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement is that the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement was forged unilaterally by Chen Chengyu. (2) The Verification Report involved in the case is merely an estimate of Chen Chengyu's investment during the cooperation. The original judgment's use of it as evidence of Chen Chengyu's investment losses lacks factual and legal basis. (a) The Verification Report is essentially an estimate or budget estimate of Chen Chengyu's production investment during the contracted mining operation. Such an estimate or budget estimate, being a production input that resulted in product output or materialization (without materializing into equipment, buildings, etc.), cannot serve as evidence of Chen Chengyu's investment losses. Chen Chengyu did not provide evidence in the original trial to show that the ore he produced was not sold or did not materialize into the basis or cost for further development of the mine. (b) According to the 5.1 Agreement, Chen Chengyu had the right to organize and implement quarrying production and sell products. Chen Chengyu's investment in mining was a production operation aimed at profit, not infrastructure construction with only input and no output. The investment losses in this case are essentially Chen Chengyu's operating losses, i.e., losses caused by investment exceeding output. Furthermore, if output exceeded input, Chen Chengyu would have no investment losses. During the mining operation period from 2005 to 2007, according to Item 3 of the Verification Report's calculation sheet, "Granite Excavation," the engineered volume was 122,560 cubic meters (rough stone). Based on the current industry standard yield rate of 8%, this amounts to 9,804.80 cubic meters. At the then market price of RMB 1,000-1,500 per cubic meter, Chen Chengyu, having invested over RMB 7 million, suffered no loss. As for the loss of anticipated profits caused by Changyu Company's rescission of the contract, since it was due to Chen Chengyu's breach (as found in the other case), it should not be supported according to law. (c) The amount of investment determined by the Verification Report should not be adopted according to law. For Chen Chengyu's request to compensate his investment losses, the calculation of investment should at least be based on relevant invoices and receipts such as wage payment slips, engineering machinery use fees, earth and rock transport fees, bank transfers, and taxes paid. The accounting firm should base its audit on legally valid invoices and accounts, not on estimates from surveying institutions. This is consistent with the rules of evidence and reality. The original judgment's reliance on survey estimates as a basis is inherently inaccurate and fails to meet the standard required for judicial decisions to support claims. In the trial of this case, the main basis for the evaluation and verification was the "Metallurgical Mine Budget Estimate Quota 2007" and the "Metallurgical Mine Construction and Installation Engineering Cost Quota 2007." Whether it was Chen Chengyu's investment, losses, or compensation from Changyu Company, all data concerning the parties' property rights were based on vague conclusions such as "budget estimates" and "preliminary estimates," undermining the seriousness of the judgment. (d) There were procedural violations in the appraisal. First, the appraisal institution for the Verification Report, Xingyi Accounting Firm, does not have the qualification for engineering cost evaluation. Second, the coal mine survey team used in the Verification Report does not have the business scope for surveying earthwork and stonework volumes. Third, the engineering cost engineer listed in the Verification Report is not an appraiser of the appraisal institution. Accordingly, the original judgment was based on unclear facts, failed to exclude illegal evidence, and had procedural violations, resulting in a clearly unfair conclusion. Changyu Company requests a retrial to amend the judgment.

Chen Chengyu responded: (1) Regarding the issue of the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement being forged. (a) Changyu Company's assertion that the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement was forged is based on subjective inference and lacks factual basis. The fact that it was not mentioned in the litigation in the relevant court in Inner Mongolia does not mean it does not exist, let alone that it was forged. At that time, Chen Chengyu could not provide the agreement because he could not find it, and mentioning it without basis would have been pointless, so he did not refer to it. (b) The short time interval between the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement and the 5.1 Agreement is normal in this case. Other agreements signed between Chen Chengyu and Changyu Company also had short signing intervals. For example, at the end of April 2005, Changyu Company issued a Letter of Commitment, and on May 1 of the same year, it signed a Supplementary Agreement terminating the internal contracting agreement. (c) The law does not have uniform requirements or formats for the form of agreements. The 5.3 Supplementary Agreement was signed at Chen Chengyu's request to ensure his investment would not suffer loss, so it is reasonable for him to be Party A. At the time, he did not pay attention to maintaining the same positions of Party A and Party B as in the 5.1 Agreement. Moreover, the positions of Party A and Party B are not important; what matters is which party they represent and whether the rights and obligations of each party are clear and corresponding. Therefore, the listing of positions is not substantive, nor is there any requirement that the listing must comply with customary rules. (d) The absence of Wang Maotang's signature on the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement does not affect the formation and validity of the agreement. The law does not require that a legal representative or responsible person must sign when signing an agreement. Therefore, whether Wang Maotang signed is not a necessary element of the agreement. Furthermore, Wang Maotang not only did not sign this 5.3 Supplementary Agreement but also did not sign the Internal Contracting Agreement dated September 26, 2004, and the subsequent Letter of Commitment and Supplementary Agreement. Accordingly, Wang Maotang's failure to sign is not evidence that the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement was forged. (e) Since the stipulation of the number of copies is not an essential clause of a contract, the absence of such a stipulation does not affect the validity of the contract. Moreover, whether Changyu Company holds the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement is a matter for Changyu Company to bear the burden of proof. The Supplementary Agreement dated May 1, 2005, terminating the internal contracting agreement also did not stipulate the number of copies. (f) Whether the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement stipulates that it has the same legal effect as the 5.1 Agreement is not a main clause of the agreement and does not affect the legal validity of the Supplementary Agreement. (g) Regarding the issue that the rights and obligations in the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement are manifestly unfair and contrary to common sense. On one hand, Changyu Company claims that Chen Chengyu's investment has been converted into commodities, realized as output value and profit. On the other hand, it claims that Chen Chengyu did not invest himself, that others invested. This is self-contradictory and cannot be justified. At the same time, since the mine required substantial investment, Chen Chengyu's request for Changyu Company to guarantee his investment is not contrary to common sense, nor are the rights and obligations manifestly unfair. If anything is unfair, it is the rescission of the agreement on the grounds of breach of contract when the huge investment was about to yield profit. (h) The jurisdiction clause in the 5.3 Supplementary Agreement was based on the fact that Chen Chengyu was still residing in Fuding City, Fujian Province at that time. After 2007, Chen Chengyu traveled seasonally between mining companies in Shanxi, Shandong, Hebei, and Inner Mongolia for work. Meanwhile, Changyu Company's objection that the jurisdiction clause, which stipulated that the case be heard by the Fuding City People's Court or the Ningde Intermediate People's Court, violates legal provisions and is invalid, is also a misunderstanding. (2) Regarding Changyu Company's objections to the Verification Report. The Verification Report was lawfully commissioned by the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court from an accounting firm. The earthwork and stonework volumes were measured by another institution commissioned by the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court. The verification procedure was lawful, the content was objective and truthful, the verification method complied with legal provisions, and the verification content fell within the business scope of the accounting firm. Changyu Company's assertion that the Verification Report cannot be used as evidence lacks factual and legal basis. Moreover, during the trial by the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court, Changyu Company was informed that if it objected to the Verification Report, it needed to submit an application for re-appraisal. However, Changyu Company did not apply for re-appraisal, indicating its acceptance of the judicial Verification Report. Additionally, the Verification Report serves as evidence of Chen Chengyu's investment losses. Changyu Company's claim that Chen Chengyu did not provide evidence of investment losses is unfounded. After contracting the mine, Chen Chengyu established four mining districts, requisitioned over 40 mu of land, built 18 kilometers of mountain roads, erected 5 kilometers of power lines, installed two transformers, built 30 rooms, dug three wells, leased 8 units of loaders and excavators, leased 10 heavy engineering vehicles, and purchased some equipment, investing a total of over RMB 13 million. When filing the lawsuit with the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court, he provided three sacks of investment receipts. Due to the large volume of receipts, which were difficult to examine, store, and file, he lawfully applied for judicial appraisal. Whether the case involved judicial audit or judicial appraisal was determined by the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court in consultation with the commissioned appraisal institution. Since some receipts were informal, a judicial verification was conducted for part of the investment. In conclusion, Changyu Company's retrial application lacks factual and legal basis. The original judgment was procedurally lawful, with sufficient evidence and correct application of law. Chen Chengyu requests that the retrial application be dismissed according to law.

Further facts found by this Court on retrial: 1. On September 26, 2004, Changyu Company (Party A) and Liu Jingyin and Chen Chengyu (Party B) entered into an Internal Contracting Agreement, stipulating that Party A would contract the white granite quarry in Qingshui County to Party B for mining, with a contracting and mining term of three years. Article 3 stipulated: "Party B must mine in accordance with a reasonable mining and unlimited mining construction plan jointly agreed upon and approved by both Party A and Party B, and shall not engage in destructive mining; otherwise, Party A has the right to terminate this agreement." Article 5 stipulated: "Party B has the right to organize and implement the production of quarry stone, pricing, and sales of products belonging to the mining area…" Article 6 stipulated: "The funds, energy, human resources, material resources, intangible assets, industrial and commercial taxes, and tax obligations required for Party B's production and sales activities shall be resolved by Party B itself; Party B and its personnel shall bear all responsibilities and obligations arising from their own actions in the course of production and business operations." Article 7 stipulated: "Party B must make diligent efforts to mine, with the first year's output reaching 10,000 cubic meters; otherwise, Party A has the right to open another mining site within Party B's contracted area." Article 10 stipulated: "Party B shall pay Party A RMB 500,000 in a lump sum as compensation for Party A's expenses in developing the white mine." Article 11 stipulated: "Party B shall pay Party A a compensation of RMB 100 per cubic meter of commercial block stone (local price) extracted from the mining area. When the price of commercial block stone (local price) rises to RMB 1,200 per cubic meter or above, compensation shall be paid at 15%; when it reaches RMB 2,000 per cubic meter or above, compensation shall be paid at 20%." Article 14 stipulated: "After three years, if Party A does not contract the mining of this mine to Party B, Party A shall compensate Party B for the fixed asset expenses invested in the mining area, with the price to be negotiated by both parties or assessed by an authoritative department." Article 16 stipulated: "This agreement shall take effect from October 15, 2004, upon signature and sealing by both Party A and Party B." 2. In April 2005, Changyu Company issued a Letter of Commitment. The content of the Letter of Commitment was: "In view of Chen Chengyu's contributions during the cooperation with Changyu Company, the company commits that after the cooperative mining plan for the mining area is determined, it will give priority to signing relevant agreements with Chen Chengyu on favorable terms." On May 1, 2005, Changyu Company and Chen Chengyu also signed a Supplementary Agreement, the content of which was: "In recognition of Chen Chengyu's contributions to the company, Changyu Company agrees to sign a new contract with Chen Chengyu on favorable terms. The Internal Contracting Agreement signed between Changyu Company and Liu Jingyin and Chen Chengyu on September 26, 2004, shall be terminated effective May 1, 2005." 3. On May 1, 2005, Changyu Company (Party A) and Chen Chengyu (Party B) signed an Agreement (i.e., the May 1 Agreement). The main contents were as follows: Article 2: "Party B's mining period is 6 years, from May 1, 2005, to April 30, 2011." Article 3: "Party B has the right to organize and implement quarry production and product sales. Party B has the obligation to rationally exploit and protect mining resources. It has the obligation to protect the mining ecological environment and to mine in accordance with the requirements of the environmental impact assessment report. It has the obligation to ensure safe production and protect workers' legitimate rights and interests. Party B shall bear all economic and legal liabilities arising from the performance or non-performance of the above rights and obligations." Article 4: "Party B must mine in accordance with a reasonable mining construction plan jointly agreed upon and approved by both Party A and Party B, shall not engage in destructive mining, and shall not transfer the mining right of the mine to others in any form; otherwise, Party A has the right to immediately terminate the contract, and the losses incurred shall be borne by Party B." Article 6: "Party B shall be responsible for resolving the funds, human resources, material resources, and taxes required for production and sales activities; Party B and its personnel shall bear all responsibilities and obligations arising from their own actions in the course of production and business operations." Article 9: "For the first three years of the mining period, Party B shall pay Party A an annual mine fee compensation of RMB 300,000. … Starting from the fourth year of the mining period, Party B shall pay Party A an annual mine fee compensation of RMB 500,000." Article 10: "If Party B fails to perform the obligations under Article 9 of this Agreement on time, Party A has the right to unilaterally terminate the contract, and the losses incurred shall be borne by Party B." Article 13: "After Party B's mining period ends, if Party B has not obtained the mining right, Party A shall appropriately compensate Party B for the expenses incurred for houses and wells invested in the mining area, with the price to be negotiated by both parties or assessed by an authoritative department." 4. On May 3, 2005, with Chen Chengyu as Party A and Changyu Company as Party B, a Supplementary Agreement (i.e., the May 3 Supplementary Agreement) was signed, stipulating that on the basis of the May 1 Agreement, the following supplementary terms were agreed upon regarding the cooperative mining of the granite stone mine. The specific content of the terms was as follows: Article 1: "Both Party A and Party B agree that, in order to ensure the full safety and no loss of all investments made by Party A during the period of cooperation with Party B in mining the stone mine, the parties agree that, regardless of whether the cooperation between the parties can continue, and regardless of whether the May 1 Agreement between the parties is valid or invalid, if Party A unilaterally rescinds or terminates the agreement, or if the Agreement is adjudicated by a court to be rescinded, terminated, or invalid, Party B agrees to liquidate and refund all of Party A's investments in accordance with the principles of fairness and reasonableness. For this purpose, either Party A or Party B has the right to apply to an appraisal institution or to a court for appraisal and assessment, and Party B shall refund Party A's investment in accordance with the appraisal and assessment results. If Party B has already applied for appraisal or assessment, the other party shall not have the right to apply again for appraisal of the appraisal report and assessment results." Article 2: "The loss referred to in the term 'Party A has the right to unilaterally terminate the contract, and the losses incurred shall be borne by Party B' as stipulated in Article 1 of the May 1 Agreement, as used in this clause, refers to business losses, and does not include Chen Chengyu's investments." Article 3: "Disputes arising from the May 1 Agreement shall be settled through negotiation between the parties; if negotiation fails, Party A and Party B agree to submit the dispute for jurisdiction and acceptance to the Fuding City People's Court of Fujian Province or the Ningde Intermediate People's Court of Fujian Province." Below this supplementary agreement were Chen Chengyu's signature and the seal of Changyu Company.

Further found: 1. During the second-instance trial, Chen Chengyu provided some production and operation vouchers, totaling 57 volumes. The vouchers reflected the following circumstances: (1) Apart from some formal invoices, the vouchers were mostly receipts, acknowledgments of receipt, personal accounting vouchers, etc. (2) The nature of the vouchers included both production expenditures and non-production expenditures. In terms of production expenditures, e.g., purchases of detonators and blasting explosives totaled over RMB 100,000; electricity expenses from July 2005 to April 2006 amounted to over RMB 29,000; purchases of a dump truck, a rock drill, an excavator, and a jeep (one each) totaled over RMB 680,000 (except for one excavator purchased by Chen Chengyu, the rest were purchased by other companies and individuals, and the excavator purchased by Chen Chengyu was not accompanied by a formal invoice). In terms of non-production expenditures, e.g., expenses for meals, tobacco and alcohol, gifts, and compensation for deaths due to liability accidents, among others, including gift expenses of over RMB 300,000. (3) The vouchers also included some content related to the sales of rough stone blocks. According to rough statistics, from March 30, 2006, to October 31 of the same year, approximately 538 cubic meters of rough stone blocks were sold, with tally sheet numbers coded 00001 and 01617 to 01697, at a sales price of RMB 1,200 per cubic meter, totaling approximately RMB 670,000 in sales revenue. (4) The vouchers also included documents such as payment vouchers, receipts, or accounting vouchers relating to rough stone processing and sales relationships between Chen Chengyu and non-party companies and certain individuals. 2. During the performance of the agreement between Chen Chengyu and Changyu Company, no personnel from Changyu Company participated in the specific mining or mine management affairs. 3. Chen Chengyu and his representatives stated that there were still many investment vouchers, but they failed to provide them after being urged during the proceedings.

Further found: 1. During the period from November 2007 to November 2008, while the Helingeer County Court and the Hohhot Intermediate Court were hearing the dispute over the cooperative mining contract between Changyu Company and Chen Chengyu, Chen Chengyu filed a counterclaim on January 28, 2008, requesting that Changyu Company return his invested capital of RMB 13 million, but he withdrew the counterclaim on May 28 of the same year. On May 29, 2008, the Helingeer County Court issued Civil Judgment (2007) He Min Chu Zi No. 428-2, holding that the agreement between Changyu Company and Chen Chengyu was in the nature of cooperative mining, with Changyu Company as the holder of the mining right and Chen Chengyu as the cooperative investment miner; the parties shared mining profits and bore mining risks; the agreement did not violate mandatory provisions of laws or regulations and was valid. During the performance of the contract, because Chen Chengyu violated the May 1 Agreement by dumping waste slag and blocking the river channel and failing to pay mining compensation on time, based on Changyu Company's claims, the judgment rescinded the May 1 Agreement between the parties. After Chen Chengyu appealed to the second instance, on November 7, 2008, the Hohhot Intermediate Court upheld the above judgment in Civil Judgment (2008) Hu Fa Min Er Zhong Zi No. 957. 2. During the period from September 2008 to February 2011, while the Hohhot Intermediate Court was hearing the case of Chen Chengyu v. Changyu Company concerning a cooperative business contract dispute, Chen Chengyu stated in his complaint that he requested Changyu Company to compensate him for his investment of RMB 9 million, based on the claim that the parties' arrangement was in name cooperation but in substance a contract for the transfer of mining operation rights and his investment during the mining period was RMB 13 million. On December 4, 2008, Chen Chengyu filed an application for judicial appraisal and assessment; on February 19, 2009, the Hohhot Intermediate Court issued a commission for appraisal to Xingyi Accounting Firm, commissioning it to verify and certify the costs of earth stripping and granite mining during Chen Chengyu's contract mining period. On May 6 of the same year, the Hohhot Intermediate Court issued a commission for survey to the Coal Survey Team, commissioning it to measure the earth and stone quantities excavated from each of Chen Chengyu's mining pits. On December 7 of the same year, Xingyi Accounting Firm issued a Verification Report, which concluded that during the cooperation period, Chen Chengyu had excavated over 50,000 cubic meters of earth and over 120,000 cubic meters of stone, incurring expenses of RMB 7,112,080. Subsequently, Chen Chengyu failed to pay the litigation fees on time, and on February 28, 2011, the Hohhot Intermediate Court ruled to treat the case as withdrawn. In the above litigation, Chen Chengyu neither mentioned nor provided the May 3 Supplementary Agreement and its stipulated content.

This Court holds that the core of this case is whether the original judgment contained errors in fact-finding and application of law, and whether Chen Chengyu's request for Changyu Company to compensate his investment losses has a factual and legal basis.

(I) Regarding the Fact-Finding Issues in the Original Judgment

The basis for the original judgment's decision that Changyu Company should bear liability for compensating Chen Chengyu's investment losses was primarily the credibility of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement and the objectivity and legality of the Verification Report. Considering the statements and evidence submissions of the parties during the original trial and retrial of this case, this Court holds that the factual basis for the original judgment that Changyu Company should bear liability for compensating investment losses is insufficient.

Regarding the determination of the authenticity of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. In September 2011, Chen Chengyu filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance based on the existence of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement with Changyu Company. In 2011, during the second-instance proceedings on jurisdictional objections in this case, Changyu Company applied to the Fujian High Court for forensic authentication of the authenticity of Changyu Company's seal on the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. After authentication by Fujian Dingli Forensic Authentication Center, the authentication opinion was that the seal was genuine. During the first-instance trial of this case, Changyu Company filed a Forensic Authentication Application with the court of first instance on May 25, 2013, again applying for authentication of the authenticity of the seal affixed on the May 3 Supplementary Agreement, and additionally applying for authentication of the sequence of the seal and text formation, the date of text formation, and the date of the paper. The court of first instance, after review, refused to support Changyu Company's renewed application for authentication of the seal's authenticity, which was not improper; however, because the sequence of the seal and text formation and the date of text formation also have significant impacts on determining the authenticity of the agreement, the court of first instance's refusal to support these aspects on the grounds that the sequence of seal and text formation does not affect the determination of the agreement's authenticity was indeed improper. In determining the authenticity of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement, although the seal affixed on the agreement was genuine, the formation of the agreement and the act of affixing the seal are relatively independent: the formation of the agreement is the reflection of the mutual expression of intent, while the affixing of the seal is the act of confirming the mutual expression of intent, i.e., the agreement. The two are interrelated but independent. In terms of evidence, a genuine seal can generally be used to infer that the mutual expression of intent was genuine. However, when there is evidence to negate or cast doubt on the genuineness of the mutual expression of intent, the authenticity of the agreement cannot be directly presumed based on the seal's authenticity alone. In other words, the seal is only prima facie evidence in proving the authenticity of the agreement. The people's court must determine the authenticity of the agreement by comprehensively considering other evidence and facts. This Court holds that the following shortcomings exist regarding the authenticity of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement in this case:

First, the May 3 Supplementary Agreement fundamentally changed the risk allocation of the May 1 Agreement, which is inconsistent with common sense, and Chen Chengyu failed to provide a reasonable explanation for this change. According to the Internal Contracting Agreement signed on September 26, 2004, by Chen Chengyu, Liu Jingyin, and Changyu Company, Chen Chengyu and the others, while obtaining the rights to quarry, price, and sell products from the mining area, were required to resolve the funds, material resources, etc., needed for production and sales activities on their own, and bore the responsibilities arising from their own actions in production and operations. Additionally, Chen Chengyu and the others were required to pay a one-time development compensation fee of RMB 500,000 and pay compensation to Changyu Company based on the price of commercial block stones at a certain percentage. It can be seen that the risk of the cooperation agreement was primarily borne by Chen Chengyu. Subsequently, the parties signed a Supplementary Agreement on May 1, 2005, deciding to terminate the Internal Contracting Agreement. Although the Supplementary Agreement contained content that Changyu Company agreed to sign a new contract with Chen Chengyu on favorable terms, the May 1 Agreement signed on May 1 of the same year still contained provisions that Chen Chengyu was responsible for the funds, human resources, material resources, and taxes for production and sales activities, and bore all responsibilities and obligations arising from its own actions. At the same time, the May 1 Agreement also granted Changyu Company the right to unilaterally terminate the agreement in cases of unreasonable mining, transfer of mining rights, or failure to pay compensation in accordance with the agreement during its performance, and stipulated that losses arising therefrom would be borne by Chen Chengyu. It can be seen that in both the earlier Internal Contracting Agreement and the later May 1 Agreement, which was signed based on Changyu Company granting Chen Chengyu favorable terms, the risk of cooperation was almost entirely borne by Chen Chengyu. However, the May 3 Supplementary Agreement made a completely opposite provision regarding the risk during the parties' cooperation period, i.e., the risk of the cooperation agreement was entirely shifted to Changyu Company. According to the content of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement, regardless of whether the agreement was valid or invalid, and regardless of whether Chan company unilaterally or a court adjudicated the agreement to be rescinded or terminated, Changyu Company was obligated to refund all of Chen Chengyu's investments except for business losses. At the same time, the Supplementary Agreement, which further deprived the other party of the right to apply for appraisal and specified the litigation jurisdiction, further shifted all risks completely to Changyu Company. This Court holds that, given that the contracting parties' positions did not change, and Changyu Company's total mine use compensation fee was only RMB 2.4 million under the agreement, the above provisions exceeded the reasonable scope of the cooperation agreement and were contrary to common sense and reason. Although Chen Chengyu explained that the signing of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement just one day after the May 1 Agreement, which fundamentally changed the content of the May 1 Agreement, was influenced by an agreement signed between Changyu Company and another person, he did not provide any supporting evidence, and his explanation has insufficient credibility.

Second, the basic content of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement contained contradictions, and Chen Chengyu could not reasonably explain them. Article 2 of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement limited the losses borne by Chen Chengyu under Article 1 of the May 1 Agreement to "business losses," in order to distinguish them from "investments" under Article 1 of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement. In fact, so-called "business losses" reflect the relationship between investment and returns, while the production and operation costs invested by Chen Chengyu in performing the agreement are essentially investments in nature. However, the May 3 Supplementary Agreement explicitly stipulated that Chen Chengyu should bear such costs on his own, making his assertion self-contradictory. During the retrial hearing, Chen Chengyu could not reasonably explain the relationship between production and operation costs, investments, and production and operation risks under normal performance of the agreement. At the same time, in his court statements, he also indicated that his claim for investment was because there was no product output in the early stage, and his excavation of the weathered layer had brought convenience to subsequent production; if there was product output, his investments and production and operation risks would be borne by him. It can be seen that the production and operation costs he claimed cannot be distinguished from investments, and operating costs were within the scope he voluntarily agreed to bear.

Third, it is inconsistent with common sense that Chen Chengyu never mentioned the May 3 Supplementary Agreement or jurisdiction issues in relevant lawsuits. In multiple related lawsuits involving Chen Chengyu and Changyu Company as opposing parties heard by the relevant People's Courts in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Chen Chengyu never mentioned that the parties had signed the May 3 Supplementary Agreement, nor did he raise any objection to the jurisdiction of the courts. Although he explained that the May 3 Supplementary Agreement could not be found at the time and was only discovered years later while sorting out personal belongings, his statements regarding the location of its discovery varied, and considering the significant impact of the content of this Supplementary Agreement on the relationship between the parties, his explanation is unreasonable.

Finally, the May 3 Supplementary Agreement also showed significant differences in form from previous contracting practices, such as the designation of Party A and Party B and the clause specifying the number of copies of the agreement.

In summary, based on the content, form, and process of formation of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement, as well as Chen Chengyu's dishonest conduct in concealing significant factual information during the original trial as found during the retrial, and taking into account Changyu Company's consistent defense that it did not voluntarily affix its seal and did not hold the agreement, this Court does not find credible the relevant contents of the May 3 Supplementary Agreement.

Regarding the acceptance and determination of the "Authentication Report". Based on the facts found by this Court during the retrial, the original trial court accepted the "Authentication Report" issued by the Xingyi Accounting Firm commissioned by the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court in the case of Chen Chengyu v. Changyu Company concerning a dispute over a cooperative business contract, and used it as evidence to determine Chen Chengyu's actual losses. This presents the following issues: First, the "Authentication Report" was prepared by the Xingyi Accounting Firm upon Chen Chengyu's application for commission by the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court. Because Chen Chengyu applied to withdraw the lawsuit, the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court had already ruled to dismiss that case. During the original trial of this case, Chen Chengyu did not apply to the original trial court for any loss assessment. The original trial court accepted and examined the "Authentication Report" provided by Chen Chengyu as expert opinion evidence, which violated the provisions of Article 76, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC and constituted an erroneous application of law. At the same time, pursuant to the provisions of Article 78 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, even if the expert opinion was lawfully commissioned by the original trial court, if a party raises an objection, the original trial court should also notify the expert to appear in court to testify; otherwise, it cannot be accepted as evidence to determine the facts of the case. Second, the "Authentication Report" in this case is an authentication of input costs and cannot serve as a basis for determining the fact of investment losses. Although the content of the "Authentication Report" lists the quantities of earth and stone excavated during Chen Chengyu's mining period and various expenses, it does not indicate whether commercial rough stone was produced from the excavated stone quantity or how much commercial rough stone was formed. That is, it does not include product output. According to the "General Geological Survey Report of the Granite Mining Area in Yushugou Village, Helingeer County, Inner Mongolia" commissioned by Changyu Company in June 2005 from the Shanxi Institute of Geological Sciences, and the "Review Opinion on the General Geological Survey Report of the Granite Mining Area in Yushugou Village, Helingeer County, Inner Mongolia" issued by Inner Mongolia Kerui Real Estate Appraisal Co., Ltd. on September 8, 2005, both reports concluded that the ore body in the cooperative mining area is stably distributed, with a thin overburden or weathered layer exposed on the surface, and the average diagrammatic rough stone yield rate of the mining area mined by Chen Chengyu was 25.03%. The above geological survey report and review opinion are basic materials for mining. As a party to the cooperative mining, Chen Chengyu should have been aware of them and did not raise any objection during the performance of the relevant mining agreement. This Court adopts this. Changyu Company's claim that part of the commercial rough stone had already been produced from the stone volume covered by the "Authentication Report" is somewhat credible and is corroborated by the facts found by this Court during the trial. Chen Chengyu's contention that no ore products were produced intentionally conceals important case facts and violates the litigation principle of good faith; this Court does not accept his statement. During the retrial, on July 20, 2014, Chen Chengyu commissioned the Inner Mongolia Geological Exploration Institute of China Metallurgical Geology Bureau to produce the "Survey Report on the Overburden of the Yushugou Granite Mining Area, Helingeer County, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region", which also investigated the rough stone yield rate of the mining area's ore body. However, this report was commissioned unilaterally by Chen Chengyu, and the surveyed pit had already been excavated; the ore body had been destroyed by mining and could not be verified. Therefore, this Court does not accept it. In summary, this Court holds that the original trial's determination of Chen Chengyu's investment losses based on the above "Authentication Report" contained errors in both fact-finding and application of law, and this Court hereby corrects them.

2. The issue of whether Chen Chengyu's claim for compensation for investment losses has factual and legal basis.

According to the facts found by this Court during the retrial, Chen Chengyu's claim for compensation for investment losses has neither a contractual basis nor a factual basis for the losses. First, regarding the contract. According to the 5.1 Agreement recognized by both parties, Changyu Company formed a legal relationship of cooperative mining development with Chen Chengyu based on its mining rights. This cooperative relationship does not violate the mandatory provisions of national laws and regulations and should be valid. Chen Chengyu's claim that he and Changyu Company formed a mining sales contract relationship and that the sales relationship is void has no factual or legal basis, and this Court does not support it. According to the relevant provisions of the 5.1 Agreement, Chen Chengyu has the right to organize and implement stone quarrying production and product sales (Article 3), and at the same time must independently arrange the funds, human resources, and materials for production and sales activities, and bear all responsibilities and obligations arising from its own causes in the course of production and operation (Article 6). He also has the obligations to protect the mine ecological environment, to mine reasonably and not engage in destructive mining, and to pay the mine fee compensation on time, among others. In addition, Article 10 of the agreement stipulates: "If Party B (Chen Chengyu) violates the obligation to pay the mine fee compensation on time, Party A (Changyu Company) has the right to unilaterally terminate the contract, and the losses caused shall be borne by Party B." According to the relevant facts found in the civil judgment (2008) Hu Fa Min Er Zhong Zi No. 957 made by the Hohhot Intermediate People's Court on November 7, 2008, during the cooperative period, Chen Chengyu not only violated the obligations under the agreement regarding ecological environmental protection and reasonable mining, but also admitted that he failed to pay the 2007 annual mine fee compensation to Changyu Company on time. Accordingly, after the 5.1 Agreement was rescinded by court judgment, according to the provisions of the above agreement, he shall bear the relevant losses himself. Second, as to the facts of loss. In the original trial, the application for retrial review, and the retrial hearing, Chen Chengyu consistently stated that during the mining period, he only had inputs and no product output, i.e., no revenue had been generated. However, when he was required by this Court to provide some investment vouchers, this Court found that the vouchers included some vouchers for the production, processing, and sale of (ore) rough stone. He did not deny this and could not provide a reasonable explanation. This Court holds that Chen Chengyu independently carried out ore production and sales, and also admitted that Changyu Company did not participate in the ore production and sales at all. The investment vouchers he submitted had serious flaws in form and content, making it difficult to determine the investment. Based on the fact that he already had ore production and sales, whether there were investment losses is also not fully supported by evidence. Furthermore, in the original trial, Chen Chengyu, as the claimant for loss compensation, not only failed to provide relevant production and operation vouchers, but also gave inconsistent statements regarding the vouchers that should have been in his possession. At times he said he had three gunny sacks of vouchers, at other times he said only three small bags. Sometimes he said the vouchers were with others and could not be obtained, sometimes he said most vouchers were lost, etc. During the retrial, after multiple reminders to Chen Chengyu to submit all production and operation vouchers within a time limit, he did not submit them to this Court. Accordingly, the factual basis for Chen Chengyu's claim for compensation for investment losses is insufficient, and this Court does not support it.

In summary, the original judgment had unclear findings of fact and erroneous application of law, and should be corrected. Pursuant to Article 207 and Article 170, paragraph 1, items (2) and (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, this Court renders the following judgment:

1. Set aside the civil judgment (2013) Min Min Zhong Zi No. 1266 of Fujian High People's Court and the civil judgment (2013) Ning Min Chu Zi No. 188 of Ningde Intermediate People's Court of Fujian Province;

2. Dismiss Chen Chengyu's claims.

The case acceptance fees for the first instance and second instance are RMB 61,585 each, totaling RMB 123,170, to be borne by Chen Chengyu.

This judgment is final.
